newsitem.title: INDIA: India political flux deepens but reforms seen safe.
newsitem.headline: India political flux deepens but reforms seen safe.

text.p: India's political confusion has deepened after a string of recent by-elections dealt blows to major parties, but the turmoil is not likely to hurt the momentum of economic reforms, analysts said on Sunday.

The analysts said an alphabet soup of groups speaking for castes, regions and religious groups was gaining strength, marking a change from the days when strong central leadership and charismatic individuals dominated India's politics.

"I don't think the instability is something to worry about. For the first time since independence (1947) we are heading for genuine federalisation," said Chandan Mitra, editor of the Pioneer newspaper.

The Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the main opposition group and the largest single party in parliament's lower house, snatched two seats from its arch-rival Congress party in by-elections earlier this month.
Regional groups won the two other seats held originally by Congress. By-elections are held either when an incumbent dies or when a seat is vacated by a lawmaker who holds a second seat.
To add to its humiliation, the once-monolithic Congress was turfed out of power in the key farming state of Punjab, where a Sikh alliance with the BJP won a landslide majority.

Congress policymakers are scheduled to meet on Monday to discuss strategy. Tainted by corruption scandals, the party suffered its worst national defeat in May 1996 and has been afflicted by strong dissent within its ranks.

The state of change has helped Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's ruling United Front coalition, which gets make-or-break support from a reluctant Congress. That tenuous partnership was forged solely to keep the BJP at bay.

"In the short term it does help the United Front," Mahesh Rangarajan, a research fellow at New Delhi's Centre for Contemporary Studies, told Reuters. "Any plans that hardliners in the Congress had of upsetting the apple cart won't gain."
The BJP had a brief taste of power after the May 1996 elections resulted in a hung parliament. It ran the central government for just 12 days and did not survive a confidence vote.
The United Front, a motley mix of centrists, free marketeers, communists and regional groups, grew even larger last week when Deve Gowda inducted two new ministers.
Regional lawmakers now have more bargaining power, but they will not reverse the economic reforms launched by the Congress party in 1991, Rangarajan said.
However there is likely to be a tug-of-war to share the spoils of power, he said.
"There is some degree of uncertainty, but there is a broad consensus on reforms. Bargaining on specifics will continue. Reforms will carry on, but with hiccups," he said.

The coalition has bickered over foreign investment in the aviation industry, the politically explosive issue of raising subsidised oil prices, and the liberalisation of the insurance market, but reform plans have not been shelved.
A large number of foreign investment proposals has been approved since Deve Gowda assumed power.

India, and the Congress party which ruled on the charisma of the Nehru-Gandhi family, entered a politically unstable phase after the assassination of Rajiv Gandhi in 1991, although it won power that year on a sympathy wave linked to his death.
Jawaharlal Nehru, his daughter Indira Gandhi and her son Rajiv between them ruled India as prime ministers for a total of 29 years since independence from Britain in 1947.
"I would say the collapse of the Congress has created a kind of political vacuum in large parts of the country," Mitra said. "It has come to be identifed with corruption and misgovernance."
"The vacuum is getting filled in different places by different groups."

In the fractured 545-seat lower house, the Lok Sabha, the United Front now has 178 direct members and claims support from outside by a dozen others, including independents. The BJP and its allies command some 194 votes. Congress has 140 members.
